second, citing scriptural statements as further proof.
Regarding the passage in the preceding section that says,
"To speak briefly, it is because of the causes of purification," etc.,
Jing says:
If one realizes that these two names give rise to various faults and afflictions,
one immediately realizes and enters the principle of the two kinds of emptiness;
this is called the cause of purification.
To observe these two is called "thoroughly knowing their specific characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa*).
That is to say, taking the four aggregates and vocal sound as their nature is called observing their specific characteristics.
The deluded attachment to these two names extensively gives rise to afflictions,
which incite karma and result in retribution;
this is termed the cause of defilement.
Because one observes this, it is called "observing the cause of affliction" (*saṃkleśa-hetu*).
Regarding the statement by Ki that it is "observing the cause of purification" (*vyavadāna-hetu*), this refers to what follows below:
"By taking this as an object, one is able to know the selflessness of persons."
It is called the "cause of purity" because it reveals that principle.

Regarding the observation of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), it is as stated below: because one contemplates the names of the two kinds [of self], the characteristic of a self (*ātman*) cannot be found.
This refers precisely to the two types of grasping at the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*).
Now that one understands this matter,
one observes the cause of defilement.
The subsequent statement, "not clearly understanding," refers to the fact that this name arises as defiled. That is to say,
because the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) arises, all phenomena arise.
Furthermore, there is another interpretation.
It is said that because the two kinds of names possess three meanings, they are called "illuminating all.
First, those who contemplate these names attain purity, as the names serve as the cause for that purity.
Second, knowing the two names as conditions that encompass all phenomena;
third, knowing the two names as defiled phenomena.
Because these three meanings are complete, it is named "reflecting all."
Regarding the phrase, "In this context, it is shown that there is no self of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya*)," etc.,
Tai states:
"Because many [erroneously] conceive the four aggregates (*skandha*) as the self."
The *Pramāṇasamuccaya* states:
"It means being able to understand that, by virtue of the designation of the four aggregates,
one falsely clings to a self-soul (*ātman*) which fundamentally lacks intrinsic nature."
However, because one falsely gives rise to conceptual constructions regarding objects such as form,
it is said that [the Bodhisattva] can sever all appearances of their own objective spheres;
therefore, he is called "one who can outshine all."
Furthermore, because of verbal expression, one grasps at phenomena by means of names;
[the teaching] causes one to realize that these names are merely provisional designations,
and that there are no separate, real phenomena, thereby entering into the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya).
This explains the first phrase.
The statement, "If one goes beyond this, even that cannot be found," explains the second phrase.
This is a general explanation regarding those who follow and engage with these two up to their arising.
If one does not clearly understand the names of these two, one gives rise to grasping toward the objects of the two spheres: persons and phenomena.
The arising and subsequent evolution of the defilements of birth and death;
that all objective appearances and various defilements are produced by the sovereign power of that [ālayavijñāna] refers to the objects of the two—
persons and phenomena— as well as the defilements of birth and death.
All arise due to the predominant power of these two names;
this explains the latter two phrases.
Below, a scriptural citation is introduced to provide further corroboration.

Regarding the statement, "It is said that these words were spoken based on this underlying intention (*saṃdhāya*)," this means that the subsequent verse was spoken based on the underlying intention of the preceding verse. As for the phrase,
"Because one clings to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena, one proceeds by clinging to a self-nature (*ātmatva*)."
The grasping at a self arises only from the conceptualization that phenomena possess a self.
To awaken to this is to awaken to that:
by awakening to the emptiness of these phenomena, one awakens to the emptiness of that person.
Furthermore, by awakening to the non-existence of these two objects— person and phenomena—
one returns to extinguish the seeds of the two types of grasping.
The preceding explanation of the first four characteristics is now complete.
From here below, the fifth [section], the "Affiliation with the Object of Focus of Yogic Mental Engagement," is explained.
Within this, first the names are raised collectively;
it is pointed out that they are to be distinguished as in the *Śrāvakabhūmi*.
The second section, the detailed explanation following the questions, is divided into two parts:
first, a general presentation of the objects of focus for purifying afflictions; second, a specific analysis thereof.
Regarding the "preceding" and "middle":
the Four Noble Truths and True Suchness (tathatā) are mentioned first because the Four Truths are extensive while True Suchness is concise.
In the sixtieth-sixth fascicle, within the section on "Resolving Difficulties," the objects of focus for purifying afflictions are presented in general.
This is distinguished separately below at the end of the preceding fascicle. First,
the Four Truths are explained individually, and subsequently, their establishment is treated collectively.
In the first part of the preceding section, the explanation of suffering (*duḥkha*) consists of three types of suffering (*triduḥkhatā*),
each presented with a formal statement,

an analogy, and a synthesis. Now, these three types of suffering are based, for the time being, on a passage in the *Yogācārabhūmi* and the *Abhidharmakośa* that concerns the three feelings (*trivedanā*) and those phenomena conducive to those three feelings.
The characteristics of the three types of suffering are distinguished as explained at length therein;
now, within this text:
What is the nature of suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*)? It refers to those formations produced by karma and afflictions that lead to future existence (*punarbhava*).
Among the karma and afflictions that bring about the three periods of time, we here cite for now the karma leading to future existence.
Furthermore, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) produced by afflictions (*kleśa*) constitute the essence of the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
Just as all conditioned phenomena produced by karma and afflictions in the present life are the suffering of conditioned existence,
so too may this [text] refer to the "subsequent" based on the sequence of cause preceding and effect following.
The various formations (*saṃskāra*) produced by karma and afflictions throughout the three periods of time are all termed "future existence" (*punarbhava*).
Therefore, it is said: "the various formations produced by the karma and afflictions of future existence.
To speak fully, these are the various formations produced by the karma and afflictions that are capable of generating [existence].
All these are the very essence of the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
Because these formations are accompanied by *dausthulya* (coarseness) and lack pliancy, their essential nature is unstable;
they lack mastery over their arising and ceasing.

Therefore, it is called the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). How is it known that this explains the suffering of conditioned existence by encompassing both karma and afflictions?
It is as stated in the following passage.
However, all that constitutes the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*) is necessarily the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).

There are, nevertheless, instances of the truth of suffering that are not the truth of origination; these include the wholesome contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena and indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) phenomena attained by Arhats, as well as the various indeterminate phenomena of maturation (*vipāka*) produced by the bodies of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Regarding the statement that "within each respective self-nature, one can produce afflictions and manifold sufferings":
the essential nature of the three types of formations (saṃskāra) is conducive to the arising of delusions and suffering.

Regarding the statement that "all that is established as being comprised within the pervasive heavy residues (dauṣṭhulya) is also called 'heavy residue,' and this is the nature of the suffering of formations (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā)": [it refers to the fact that] these formations are characterized by a state of dysfunction that pervades all conditioned existence.
This refers to the fact that, with respect to those various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the three natures,
they universally serve as the basis for both afflictions (*kleśa*) and manifold sufferings;
that is, there is the quality of being unpliant due to affliction.

Because these conditioned formations (saṃskāra) follow and persist throughout all three natures, causing their activity to be unstable, they constitute the nature of the suffering of conditioned formations (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā).
Furthermore, when those formations give rise to the suffering of suffering (duḥkha-duḥkhatā) and the suffering of change (vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā), [they likewise constitute suffering].
Furthermore, there are two types of suffering associated with an untrainable nature that follow those actions, causing their conduct to be unstable;
these are also called "actions.
Moreover, this suffering of action (saṃskāraduḥkhatā) pervades all three types of sensation.
When the three feelings are experienced, they are all characterized by the heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). If this is so,
why is it said exclusively that the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) is its conditioned suffering?
To resolve this doubt, it is said:
"In this way, the nature of this heaviness (*dausthulya*) is clearly manifest within the sensation of equanimity;
however, it is only the sensation of equanimity that is described as the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*)."
Regarding the statement that "the other two feelings are disturbed by craving and aversion, and this coarse heaviness (dauṣṭhulya) of suffering is not easily understood":
it is said that pleasant feeling is [suffering] through transformation because it is disturbed by craving.

Painful feeling (duḥkhā-vedanā) is taught as the suffering of suffering (duḥkha-duḥkhatā) because it is disturbed by aversion (pratigha); although it is also the suffering of conditioned existence (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā), its characteristic is difficult to discern.
Next, a simile is provided below; the present simile is according to the text.
Question: Just as one gives rise to aversion toward the pleasure of others when one’s own pleasure arises, [how is this so?]
Ignorance arises simultaneously with both one’s own and others’ pleasure;
just as it arises not only toward painful sensations but also toward attachment—namely, the two types of craving:
the desire for acquisition and the desire for separation.
Since attachment arises at the beginning, middle, and end of equanimity (*upekṣā*),
why is it said exclusively that pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) is disturbed by attachment (*rāga*) and painful feeling (*duḥkha-vedanā*) is disturbed by aversion (*pratigha*)?
The following text contains two successive sections to resolve this objection.
The first states: "Although each individual sensation gives rise to the three delusions..."
However, pleasure that accords with one's feelings generally gives rise to craving and attachment;
painful sensations generally give rise to aversion;
and regarding neutral sensations—which are characterized by the suffering inherent in conditioned existence—one generally gives rise to ignorance and the four inversions.
Furthermore, this second section explains that foolish worldlings,
due to many causes, give rise to craving for pleasant feelings and engage in the three types of unwholesome conduct,
thereby being born in the hells; moreover, due to many causes, they give rise to craving for pleasure and experience suffering throughout all realms, undergoing the eight types of suffering.
For the most part, aversion arises from painful feelings;
one performs the three types of unwholesome conduct and is reborn in the various evil destinies.
Within neutral feelings, for the most part, the aforementioned ignorance and inversions arise.
It refers to two kinds of suffering: namely,
the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*) arising from the two types of craving based on pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*),
and the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkha*) arising from aversion (*pratigha*) based on painful feeling (*duḥkha-vedanā*).
Furthermore, the arising of non-renunciation through ignorance gives rise to the suffering of change; that is,
due to ignorance, one gives rise to craving and is unable to feel weary of it or relinquish it.
Regarding the arising of the practice of non-abandonment from birth as the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*):

as for the arising of the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkha*), it likewise arises from ignorance; through the arising of hatred, the practice of non-abandonment toward the suffering of suffering is produced.
Therefore, the following section concludes that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, established only three types of root afflictions.
From the phrase "based on this underlying intention" onwards, the commentary explains the observation of the characteristics of the three types of sensation (*vedanā*) according to the sūtra.
If one can thus truly contemplate the nature of impermanence and below that,
contemplate the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), gradually severing perversions;
these conditioned phenomena are the matter of the Noble Truth of Suffering in its ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).
The fact that the noble truth of suffering consists in the ultimate sense in the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) means that all noble ones (*ārya*),
starting from the lowest level, employ the method of "elevating the superior to illustrate the inferior" (*ūrdhva-ādharopamāna*);
thus, they do not give rise to any delight within the truth of suffering.
Next, the truth of origination (samudaya-satya) is distinguished.
The principle of origination—that is, the truth of origination—is itself suchness (tathatā).
However, it is designated as the noble truth of origination by means of establishing the names "karma" and "afflictions" (kleśa) based on their defining characteristics.
Therefore, it is said: "by way of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇayukti*).
Alternatively, the common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of arising (*samudaya*) may be called "reasoning" (*yukti*);
within this, that which is preeminent is termed "preeminent reasoning" (*viśeṣayukti*).
The following section distinguishes the Truths of Cessation and the Path according to the text.
Next, it distinguishes the intent behind the establishment of the Four Noble Truths:
it is intended to cause the practitioner to know suffering, abandon the origin [of suffering], realize cessation, and cultivate the path.

they are, in fact, limitless.
Furthermore, this is intended to bring about understanding, which will later be explicitly shown as the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*).
Among the eight types of suffering, the suffering of birth is the coarsest; next are old age and sickness, followed by death;
continuing thus up to the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*).
The first five sufferings constitute the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*).
The next two [aspects] are the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkha*);
