"All contaminated contacts (*sāsrava-sparśa*) can serve as nutriment for joy and pleasure."
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* also states:
"When the contaminated [consciousnesses] first apprehend an object, they grasp joy (*sukha*), pleasure (*saumanasya*), and the beneficial equanimity (*upekṣā*) that can function as nutriment.

The intent of this statement is to reveal that the eight contaminated consciousnesses of the three realms all possess contact that grasps joy, pleasure, and beneficial equanimity, thereby nourishing and benefiting the body.
This is the essence of the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*).
If it induces suffering or grief, or if it is a neutral contact that does not benefit, its essence is not a nutriment,
because it does not provide sustenance.
Therefore, the *Cheng weishi lun* (Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only) states:
"Although this contact (*sparśa*) is associated with all consciousnesses, its character as 'nutriment' (*āhāra*) is particularly predominant in relation to the six consciousnesses;
this clearly demonstrates that the nutriment of contact pervades all eight consciousnesses."
The *Mi-hui Tian-qin She-lun* (Secret Explanation of Vasubandhu’s *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*), fascicle three, states:

"Among these, the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*) pertains to the six groups of consciousness; because it nourishes by means of its superior engagement with coarse and manifest objects, it does not aggregate other types of contact."
There is another interpretation which holds that only the contact (*sparśa*) co-arising with the six consciousnesses constitutes the substance of nutriment.

This master asserts that only that which can induce its own co-arising joy, affection, and so forth is designated as nutriment; therefore, it is not the contact of the seventh or eighth consciousnesses.
Nevertheless, according to various texts, the second interpretation is superior.
Regarding "nutriment of volition" (*cetanāhāra*), the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"It refers to contaminated volition that arises simultaneously with desire."
Furthermore, it is said that although this volition is associated with all consciousnesses,
its function as "nutriment" is most predominant when it belongs to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
This statement precisely clarifies that within the three realms, volition associated with all eight contaminated consciousnesses (*sāsrava-vijñāna*) takes desirable objects and benefits the body.
All [masters] consider this to be the substance of food.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (fascicle 57) and Vasubandhu’s *Triṃśikā-vijñapti-bhāṣya* state in secret agreement:
"Objects in the future serve as conditions that benefit consciousness."
It is called the nutriment of volition (*manahsaṃcetanāhāra*) because the mental intention (*manasikāra*) has a superior aspiration toward its object.
For this reason, it is stated in the *Ninety-four [Verses]*:
"If it is on the level of the mental ground (*manobhūmi*), the volition that can encounter the object is called 'volition of mental encounter' (*manaḥsampratighasaṃcetanā*)."
It is able to serve as nutriment for all [beings] by focusing their hope upon objects of affection.

Furthermore, there is another interpretation: the volition (cetanā) associated with the six consciousnesses—specifically that which pertains to the outflows (sāsrava)—is the essence of the nutriment of volition, as it seeks beneficial objects for the sake of the body.
Seventh and eighth: this is not so, because they lack the characteristic of mental activity (*ākāra*).
As for the various sources stating that [the mind] is associated with the mental faculty (*manas*), [it refers to the following].
Because it universally takes the future as its object and because that [future] is most excellent,
there is also volition (cetanā) that anticipates present objects; therefore,
it is admitted to be associated with all five consciousnesses.
There is an interpretation that the food of volition (manahsaṃskāra-āhāra) is associated only with the sixth consciousness,
because all sources state that it takes only the future as its object;
although there are three interpretations of this, the second is superior.
Regarding the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*), the *Cheng weishi lun* states:
"It refers to contaminated consciousness (*sāsrava-vijñāna*).
Although this consciousness pervades the essential nature of all consciousnesses, the eighth consciousness (*aṣṭama-vijñāna*) is predominant in the sense of being a nutriment."
This reveals that the nutriment of consciousness (vijñānāhāra) encompasses the eight contaminated (sāsrava) consciousnesses throughout the three realms.
Next, it distinguishes their presence or absence according to the destinies (gati).
It says: "From coarse physical nutriment up to those who are not great narakas..."
Jingyun says:
It is said that among the mountains, in a vast open field, there is a solitary small hell where coarse food exists.
This refers to the previous statement that there is no solid food (kavadīkāra-āhāra) in the hells.
Because the suffering experienced within the great hells is so extreme, there is no solid food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) there.
Tái says:
"Solid food has both coarse and subtle varieties; the coarse variety pervades all five destinies."
According to this text, it excludes only the great *kavaḍīkāra-āhāra* (solid food).
Within the great *kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*, there are also subtle forms;
as stated in the fifth chapter of the *Maulī Bhūmi*:
In the hells, there exists a subtle form of edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*);
that is to say, because of a subtle wind, edible food pervades all the hells.
First, in the second section concerning the establishment and refutation [of the four foods], the initial question and answer establish the four foods through their respective refutations and proofs.

Regarding the question, "The middle four [powers] arise from mastery over the mind through the supernormal powers (abhijñā)," this means that by the power of the supernormal knowledge of the movement of the physical body (ṛddhividhi-jñāna-abhijñā),
one causes the force of the karma that projects longevity to increase, thereby attaining a long life and remaining for a long duration.
Alternatively, the supernormal power of mastery over the mind (*cetaḥ-prabhāva-ṛddhi*) is precisely the power of the ultimate meditative concentration (*prāntakoṭika-dhyāna*).
It extends that residual karma so that its efficacy becomes superior, thereby drawing forth the life-force to remain for a long duration.
Regarding the sixth [point], "by means of wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral mental orientations (*manasikāra*)," etc.:
Jingyun: Through the mental attention (*manasikāra*) of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the six consciousnesses are induced to arise repeatedly and without cessation,
grasping the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) produced by external, internal, common, and uncommon karma.
Ji says: This refers to the karma of the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), as in the third chapter of the *Mūla-bhūmi*,
which brings about [the world] for one kalpa or more.
When this karma is performed,
it is brought forth by means of mental attention (*manasikāra*) of the three natures;
it is capable of drawing forth the dharmas of the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) and causing them to abide without interruption.
For example, mountains, rivers, and the like are said to arise from collective karma (*sādhāraṇa-karman*), while fields, houses, and the like arise from non-collective karma (*asādhāraṇa-karman*).
Thus, Master Tai [Hui] maintained that there are two kinds: the collective and the non-collective.
Regarding the two types of shared [elements]: first, those that are shared within the shared, such as mountains, rivers, and so forth;
second, those that are shared-within-the-shared-but-unshared, such as houses and so forth.
Regarding the two types of unshared [elements]: first, those that are unshared-within-the-unshared.

Just as one's own eye-faculty is not a condition for others, these two are "unshared within the shared. This is like the sense-object that supports the faculty within the body, which appears similar to being a condition for others;
herein, there are two types of "within the shared."

The answer to the text, although it states that "conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) endure through these seven kinds of causes and conditions, even up to causing the continuity of conditioned phenomena to endure," is a general response. To take,
for example, edible food (kavaḍīkārāhāra):
Some consume roots, medicinal herbs, flowers, fruits, mud, stones, fire, iron, and so forth;
through these various means, they cause their conduct to endure.
By means of such solid food (*kavadīkārāhāra*), the food of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*) is gratified.
Because the nutriment of consciousness (vijñānāhāra) is pleasurable, it increases joy and bliss;
contact associated with joy and bliss constitutes the nutriment of contact (sparśāhāra);
and volition constitutes the nutriment of volition (manosaṃcetanāhāra).
Therefore, all four nutriments cause the various formations to endure through various modes.
Furthermore, these four nutriments respectively sustain specific meanings:
first, physical vigor.
Second, joy and pleasure;
third, focused aspiration toward desirable objects;
fourth, the abiding and non-destruction of the sense faculties, the primary elements, life-force, and warmth that serve as the basis for those three.
The following section has five parts, which explain the reasons why [beings] are caused to abide by means of various approaches.
First, these various foods cause sentient beings to abide; this is easy to grasp and is known equally by both the foolish and the wise.
Therefore, food is established as a separate category.
Second, it prevents the emaciation of the faculties and increases the great elements;
that is, it provides nourishment such as ghee and fats.
Third, it is that which causes diseases to be cured, namely medicinal herbs and the like.
Fourth, there are long-lived sentient beings who do not die prematurely while eating;
they may also consume elixirs of immortality.
Sentient beings with long lifespans must repeatedly take medicinal substances over a long period to assist their prior vitality;
these medicines constitute edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).
If they do not continue to consume them, they will meet an untimely death.
Fifth, these various foods facilitate entry into the path by enabling the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
That is to say, through edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*), one is able to cultivate the foundation of mindfulness of the body;
through contact as food (*sparśāhāra*), one is able to cultivate the foundation of mindfulness of feelings (*vedanā*).
By means of the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*), one is able to cultivate the application of mindfulness to the mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*);
by means of the nutriment of volition (*saṃskārāhāra*), one is able to cultivate the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Next, the establishment of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is analyzed.
This refers to the possibility that beings may abide for a certain duration of life;
that is to say, the gods of the form realm (*rūpadeva*) and others abide according to the lifespan they have experienced, without depending on food or drink.
This is stated with respect to the happy destinies (*sugati*), where abiding depends solely upon the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
There are those in the miserable realms who subsist solely by the power of their life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*),
such as the hungry ghosts (*preta*).
Third, the specific characteristics of edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) are distinguished.
In this section, first there is a general heading followed by a detailed explanation of the reasons.
This consists of three parts;
the first uses the four types of sensory objects (*viṣaya*) to distinguish between what constitutes nutriment and what does not.
Next, regarding edible objects, the distinction between nutriment and non-nutriment is established based on whether pleasure arises at the time of ingestion;
subsequently, the distinction between nutriment and non-nutriment is established based on whether pleasure arises at the time of ingestion.
Regarding the first case, it is said that odors, tastes, and tangibles [are nutriment] when they are being properly digested and transformed, thereby nourishing the embryo and so forth.
Jingyun asked:
"The essence of the four objects, such as form and so forth, is pervasive and mutually interfused; this is precisely the dharma of being in the same location without separation.
When they reach the stage of dissolution and transformation, all four undergo dissolution and transformation."
What was once white is now yellow;
what was once fragrant is now foul;
what was once sweet is now bitter.
If the former [nutriments] are solid and the present one is warmth, why is visible form alone not considered nutriment? Furthermore,
when falling into the receptacle for digestion (pakvāśaya) and undergoing the process of transformation,
the four objects— visible form and the rest— are not individually discerned by the four consciousnesses, such as visual consciousness.
Why is it that one perceives only fragrance and so forth, yet does not perceive visible form?
The explanation is:
at the very moment of transformation through ripening, although the three consciousnesses do not apprehend the three objects.
By comparing what precedes with what follows,
one knows that only odors and so forth constitute substantial food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*). Why is this so?
It is like when rice is being brought;
before it has entered the mouth, one sees the color of the rice and this does not merely alleviate hunger and thirst.
Therefore, color is not food.
Later, when food enters the mouth and is chewed and swallowed,
the nose, tongue, and body consciousnesses perceive odors, flavors, and tangibles;
although they have not yet undergone transformation into the long-term faculties and great elements, at that moment they are able to quench thirst.
Since those three objects [of taste, smell, and touch] satisfy thirst at the very moment of swallowing,
it is verified that later, during the stage of digestion and transformation,
only smell, taste, and touch nourish the sense faculties and fulfill their function as food.
These are not the objects of form (*rūpa*).
Master Ji says:
"The three objects [of smell, taste, and touch] possess the quality of increase and decrease."
The substance of the form-object (*rūpa-viṣaya*) cannot increase through coarseness.
Next, it says:
"If all material objects were merely called the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*)."
Jingyun: When the three consciousnesses perceive their respective three objects,
each of those three consciousnesses constitutes the essence of the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*).
Alternatively, one may take the number [of mental factors] associated with those three consciousnesses as the substance of the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*).
At that time, because the three objects have not yet been able to provide nourishment, they are not called "edible food" (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).
Master Ji says:
Because this grasping causes the mind to rejoice,
it is the mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśa*)— as a factor of consciousness—
that constitutes the essence of the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*), not the grasping of sensory objects.
The remainder of the text may be understood.
Regarding the fourth section, which distinguishes the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*):
from "contact" up to "consciousness," one should apply the four alternatives as appropriate.
There may be that which is contact but not nutriment;
namely, a portion of contact associated with painful feeling, mental grief, and equanimity.
There may also be that which is neither nutriment nor contact.
The first refers to that which is capable of nourishing the sense faculties and the primary elements through the three types of edible food.
Alternatively, there are instances where something is contact yet is also seen as food;
this refers to contact that provides benefit.
The two feelings of joy and pleasure, as well as a portion of equanimity, the faculties, the great elements, and so forth,
are either not contact or are not nutriment; that is to say,
those things which are not nutriment include the three types of nutriment— edible food, volition, and consciousness.
There may be volition that is not nutriment;
this refers to that which, taking the past or the future as its object, cannot sustain or benefit the faculties and the great elements.
Or there may be nutriment that is not volition.
That is to say, there are the other three nutriments.
There is that which is volition (*cetanā*) and is also a nutriment;
namely, volition accompanied by desire (*chanda*) that takes as its object the future benefit of the faculties (*indriya*) and the great elements (*mahābhūta*).
The fourth phrase refers to the remaining three non-nutriments; or,
there may be consciousness that is not a nutriment.
Regarding the third case, where the consciousness that is supported cannot grow:
either the food is this [nutritive essence] while the consciousness is something else— referring to the other three types of nutriment—
or it is the third phrase.
That which serves as a support for consciousness and benefits the faculties and the great elements is [the first category].
The fourth phrase refers to those among the aforementioned three that are not sustenance.
There are twelve ways of explaining phenomena that have maturation (*vipāka*) and those that do not.
Within this, first there is the analysis of those things that possess maturation (*vipāka*);
next, the analysis of dharmas with maturation in relation to feeling (*vedanā*);
and finally, the analysis of maturation in relation to karma.
The beginning and middle [of this section] have two parts:
first, a general presentation of the three phrases; second, a detailed explanation of the three phrases.
Within that, the first part, which analyzes the dharmas that possess maturation (*savipāka*), is divided into two.
First, the analysis of dharmas that possess maturation;
second, the analysis of dharmas that lack maturation.
Regarding the former, Jing says:
It is said that, briefly stated, there are dharmas with maturation (savipāka),
and secondly, there are dharmas without maturation (avipāka).
Regarding the former, Jing says:
To speak briefly regarding dharmas that possess maturation (*vipāka*):
"the outflows (*āsrava*) and those associated with outflows (*sāsrava*)" indicates the essential nature of these dharmas.
Only when three conditions are fulfilled does a dharma possess maturation.
First, it must possess power;
second, it must not be subject to harm;
third, its enjoyment must remain inexhaustible.
The following explains three meanings.

Among the contaminated (*sāsrava*), those other [than the defilements] are termed "powerless. Within the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), this refers to factors that are not afflictions, such as sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*), as well as non-obscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) phenomena.
All are termed "powerless.
T'ai says:
"Unwholesome dharmas, because their nature is that of abandonment, have no maturation."
Wholesome states with outflows (*sāsrava-kuśala*) have no maturation (*vipāka*) because they sever the outflows;
one should not say that the outflows are already severed merely by virtue of the cessation of their substance.
Furthermore, that which is an outflow may also be termed "with outflows."
Therefore, it is said that "outflows are severed.
Second, the analysis of the dharma of maturation (*vipāka*).
Master Zhongjing says:
Regarding the statement that at the time of death, the final moment of consciousness is a *vipāka* (maturation) dharma:
this means that the mind at the moment of death (*maraṇa-citta*) is exclusively the *ālayavijñāna*, which is neutral (*avyākṛta*) as a maturation.
Regarding the statement "the mind immediately following the linking of rebirth" (*pratisandhi-anantara-citta*), this occurs at two distinct times.
First is the mind at the initial moment of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*),
because it is the means for the subsequent retribution following the first linking of existence (*pratisandhi*).
Second is the mind at the moment of birth (*upapatticitta*).
This is because it is the fundamental basis for the subsequent retribution following the second linking of existence (*pratisaṃdhi*).
Question: Is there mental consciousness at the moment of death and rebirth?
Regarding this, there are two conflicting views in the West (India).
One [teacher] says there are none.
If that is so, why does it say only "six stages" within the *acittikabhūmi* (the stage without mind)?
The answer is: because of death and rebirth.
Because the mental formations (*citta-saṃskāra*) are subtle due to the pressure of extreme suffering,
they are not mentioned separately as they are subsumed within the state of mindless fainting.
Second, it is said that at both the moment of death and the moment of rebirth, there is invariably the presence of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Finally, regarding the statement here that death and rebirth are exclusively maturation (*vipāka*):
because within this state the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is subtle, it is designated as "maturation" by way of the *ālayavijñāna*.
The initial explanation is considered superior as it accords with the Abhidharma.
Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 80, states:
"When all Arhats are about to enter the nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*)."
First, one enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) to extinguish the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*);
subsequently, abiding within the indeterminate mind of maturation (*vipākavijñāna*),
one finally attains parinirvāṇa.
Regarding the statement "excluding the indeterminate mind of preparatory application" (*prayoga-avyākṛta-citta*):
all four types of indeterminate minds that are directed toward and induced by attention are collectively termed the indeterminate mind of preparatory application.
Tai says:
According to the commentary by the son of the Most Victorious One (Vasubandhu) and the teachings of Master Śīlabhadra and others,
the final moment of consciousness at the time of death is the ālayavijñāna as maturation (vipāka).
The final mind of the intermediate state (antarābhava) gives rise to the continuity of rebirth-linking.

From the mind that links rebirth at the end of the life-span of the intermediate state, there arises in immediate succession the subsequent mind of the intermediate state; this is called the "mind of immediate succession of rebirth-linking."
This is also the maturation (*vipāka*) of the ālayavijñāna;
because one faints at the time of birth, the six consciousnesses do not function.
At the moment of death and rebirth, it is solely the ālayavijñāna that persists.
The mind at the moment of death, at the end of life, does not seek retribution because it ceases spontaneously; thus, it is merely a result of maturation (*vipāka*).
The final mind of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is the means for taking birth, as it seeks to undergo existence through rebirth.
It is not a defiled mind because it does not cease spontaneously. Furthermore,
if one attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarābhava) and does not seek rebirth in an existence,
and because all afflictions have been severed, the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) also ceases at the end of life.
Furthermore, Master Śīlabhadra said:
"The sixth consciousness either relies upon the five consciousnesses,
or it relies upon the five consciousnesses as its object-condition."
The fiftieth [verse] states:
"Because it relies upon or is taught by [the present], it takes the past and future as objects;
at the initial moment of birth, the five consciousnesses do not exist, nor does it take teachings as its object."
Therefore, there is no consciousness [there].
Although at other times in the formless realm one does not rely on the five sensory consciousnesses or on teaching,
it is because of the power of having repeatedly practiced relying on names while previously in the desire realm.
In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), at other times, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises alone.
At the initial moment of receiving retribution, the mind of retribution (*vipākacitta*) must necessarily arise;
because the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and the mind of retribution arise spontaneously, [the mental consciousness] is able to arise.
The resultant consciousness of the six sense-cognitions arises dependent upon other conditions;
because at the moment of initial birth there are no such conditions, the resultant consciousness of the six sense-cognitions does not arise.
From this point begins the first experience of birth.
Thereafter, all spontaneously arising minds that abide in their own nature are the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).
This excludes the wholesome and afflicted minds of the six consciousnesses, as well as the other six consciousnesses’ preparatory and four types of neutral minds.
The six consciousnesses, being born of retribution, arise due to other conditions and do not arise spontaneously and constantly;
they are also minds that are neutral through application (*prayoga-avyākṛta*).
The seventh consciousness, which is defiled, is also included therein.
Apart from these, all remaining [states] are termed the mind abiding in its own nature within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
Even when the mind is free from desire, the mind abiding in its own nature within the fundamental consciousness continues to function accordingly.
Excluding the wholesome states of the lower stages and the four types of neutral minds resulting from application,
it should be understood that this fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is also a maturation (*vipāka*).
At the time of detachment from desire, its maturation remains the same as it was prior to that detachment.
Therefore, it is said that [the ālayavijñāna] is also a superior friend. The *Vyākhyāyukti* states:
"The fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) operates constantly and need not be analyzed.
The sixth consciousness, when it is a retributive neutral mind, is called the maturation-consciousness (*vipākacitta*)."
It functions constantly throughout the three periods of death, rebirth, and abiding in its own nature;
because it is not clearly manifest at the time of death and rebirth,
it is the ripening consciousness (*vipākacitta*).
In the "Basic Section" (*Maulī Bhūmi*), among the six states in which the six consciousnesses do not function, it is not stated that they do not function at the time of death and rebirth.
Therefore, we know that at the time of death and rebirth, there exists the retributive mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
From the time of birth until death, all minds that arise spontaneously by their own nature are the maturation (*vipāka*) of the six consciousnesses;
this is because the other three types of neutral states, as well as wholesome and afflicted states, arise through applied effort (*prayoga*) and are not spontaneous by their own nature.
Therefore, it must be excluded.
Third, the analysis of the dharmas born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
It is asked: if those that arise from the maturation of all seeds are termed "dharmas born of maturation," [then what of this?]
The seeds of the three natures, derived from their supporting consciousnesses,
are all termed "maturation" (vipāka).
From these seeds, the phenomena of the three natures arise.
All are termed "ripening phenomena" (*vipāka-dharma*). Zhongjing says:
"Furthermore, in all cases, it refers to the final dying-consciousness and the subsequent first and second moments of the continuous stream of consciousness, and so forth."
The death-existence (cyuti-bhava) is called the "final ceasing mind.
Once the death-existence has ceased, the intermediate existence (antarābhava) first arises in succession to it; this is called the "first connecting mind" (pratisandhi-citta).
When the birth-existence (upapatti-bhava) arises in succession to that intermediate existence, it is called the "second connecting mind."
All are exclusively associated with neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*).

Regarding the statement "excluding the initial moment of the continuity up until that which is comprised within maturation (*vipāka-grāhaka*)," this excludes both the initial moment of the continuity of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the mind at the moment of birth (*upapatti-citta*).
Because these feelings within the mind are experienced in all places, they are comprised of maturation (*vipāka*).
It should be understood that other feelings of pleasure and pain are likewise all produced from maturation.
Excluding the initial moment of consciousness in that intermediate state (*antarābhava*),
from the second moment of consciousness onward, the consciousness of the intermediate state encompasses both suffering and pleasure;
it is born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
Excluding the mind at the moment of birth,
from the second moment onward, it belongs to the state of "original existence" (pūrvabhava).
Within this state, the mutual arising of the three types of sensation constitutes "that which is born of maturation" (vipākaja).
The following explains the meaning of "arising from maturation" (*vipākaja*).
Regarding the statement, "Just as seeds are comprised within maturation, so too [the consciousness] arises from maturation":
seeds of the three natures (wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral) are collectively termed "maturation" with respect to the supporting consciousness (*āśraya-vijñāna*).
When these seeds give rise to manifest activity (*pravṛtti*), it is termed "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*).
Regarding the statement that one is born in the hells (*naraka*) and so forth until there is a continuity of suffering and mental distress born of maturation:

in the birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*) of the hells, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is definitively absent; there is only the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) and the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
From the second moment following the immediate [rebirth], there is a continuous succession of suffering born of maturation (*vipākaja*), consisting of physical pain and mental grief;
it was only previously, among the twenty-two faculties, that the suffering of the hells was explained.
Extreme sorrow is also called suffering (*duḥkha*).
This is stated according to what exists fundamentally.
As for the present statement that "suffering and sorrow continue uninterruptedly following maturation (*vipāka*"), it refers to this.
Regarding the statement that "just as one enters the existence of birth from the existence of becoming,
so it is for those born in the hells," and so forth: at the moment of initial birth,
whether in the realms of suffering or pleasure, or among ghosts and animals, there is likewise a continuity of equanimity immediately followed by suffering and mental distress.
Regarding the statement: "If one is born among humans, there is no certainty [of remaining so]; even when emerging from below, there is no certainty;
immediately following the maturation (vipāka), at times there may be suffering, mental distress, and so forth."
When beings of the desire realm, whether humans or devas, first undergo birth,
they enter either sorrow or suffering after the feeling of equanimity,
or they enter joy or pleasure, or they return to equanimity.
The statement that "once one has been born in the fourth dhyāna or above, there is only the ripening (vipāka) of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling" is a general formulation;
what follows below provides its specific analysis.
Regarding the statement, "Therefore, one should know that it is included within [the category of] 'attainment'":
in reality, this is merely equanimity (upekṣā) designated by the general names of joy (prīti) and bliss (sukha).
This is because this feeling of equanimity can benefit both body and mind.
Regarding the statement that those various wholesome karmas are also called "having desirable maturation":
the wholesome mental karma of the fourth dhyāna and above is associated exclusively with equanimity (*upekṣā*).
The manifestation of karmic retribution is also called "lovely maturation" (*iṣṭavipāka*).
Therefore, it is previously named "vast joy and bliss.
Tai says:
The second continuous mind arises following the first continuous mind;
therefore, it is said that "the second continuous mind follows the first.
This is according to the commentaries of the *Jinaputra* and others.
Only the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is maturation (*vipāka*);
the six consciousnesses, being of all three moral natures, are all born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
This is according to the interpretation of the commentary by Guṇamitra.
The six consciousnesses that are resultant minds (*vipāka-citta*) are both matured results (*vipāka*) and born of maturation (*vipākaja*).

Regarding the statement that from the fourth dhyāna upward they are also called "agreeable maturation" (*iṣṭa-vipāka*), the commentary explains it as follows: [This refers to] the maturation [of karma].
Because one takes the meditative joy and bliss as a means to embrace the feeling of equanimity in the fourth dhyāna,
those wholesome karmas of the fourth dhyāna are also called "desirable maturation" when the feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure manifests.
Another explanation is that the ease and bliss mentioned in the fourth dhyāna are intended to encompass the joy and bliss of the [lower] stages extensively.
Bei says: "The preceding text only discusses [the absence of] sorrow, joy, and pleasure within the hells.
Why, then, do suffering and sorrow arise here?
The explanation says:
In the preceding passage concerning edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*), it was stated that there is no sorrow and so forth because the reference was to the great hells (*mahānaraka*).
Now, however, it is stated that there is sorrow because the reference is to the peripheral hells (*pratyekanaraka*).
Since these references are distinct, what contradiction is there?
The Tripitaka Master says:
In places of pure suffering, there is the designation of "suffering" within the mental faculty (manobhūmi), namely the faculty of grief (daurmanasyendriya).
This is not logically contradictory, just as in the Third Dhyāna, pleasure exists within the mental faculty.
The following section distinguishes the maturation (*vipāka*) in relation to karma.
Regarding the statement, "the unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) maturation fruit obtained from white-with-white-maturation karma," this sentence serves as the general summary.
The phrase "appropriated by seeds of exclusively desirable sensation" clarifies that the cause is white.
The phrase "one should know that it is exclusively desirable and exclusively agreeable" clarifies that the fruit is white.
Although this objection does not specifically point to the wholesome karma of the three realms as the substance of white karma,
its intent effectively takes the wholesome karma of the three realms as that substance.
By analogy with what is explained below regarding mixed black-and-white karma, which takes both wholesome and unwholesome karma as its substance, [the same principle applies here].
Regarding mixed black-and-white karma:
one immediately knows that the wholesome karma— both its fundamental roots and its preparatory means— arisen when one has not yet abandoned desire in the desire realm is unmixed with evil,
as well as the wholesome karma arisen at the time of abandoning desire.
These are both the essence of white-and-white karma (*śukla-śukla-karman*).
According to this passage in the *Abhidharmakośa*, it is explained that wholesome karma of all three realms constitutes the essence of white-and-white karma.
However, in one passage of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, it is stated that only wholesome karma of the form and formless realms constitutes white-and-white karma.
Regarding the statement that "black-black karma" is the opposite of this:
it refers to the undertaking of unwholesome roots and their preparatory applications— karma that is purely unwholesome—
which brings about the two types of retribution for the miserable realms, both general and specific.
It also takes as its essence the karma that results in the distinct retribution of painful sensations within the realms of humans and devas.
In another passage of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, it states that the "black-black karma" refers to unwholesome karma that brings about rebirth in the evil destinies.
It is said that karma with both black and white maturation also has two types.
Regarding the feeling produced by maturation:
it is as when one performs a wholesome action with unwholesome means.
Just as when one performs unwholesome karma with wholesome means,
these two are collectively categorized as mixed karma;
when the fruit is subsequently obtained, one experiences a mixture of suffering and pleasure.
According to the Abhidharma, the meaning of this passage is as follows:
it is said therein that there may be cases where something is black in terms of its application (*prayoga*) but white in terms of its intention (*āśaya*).
There are cases where, due to the intention at the time of skillful means, that which is white becomes black;
these are collectively subsumed as "mixed karma of black and white.
This is stated in a passage within a single section of the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
Only those meritorious karmas arising at a time when one has not yet abandoned desire are taken as the substance of "black-and-white" karma,
because unwholesome karma exists as its adversary.
According to that very text, the wholesome karma of the desire realm belonging to one who has already abandoned the objects of desire is not subsumed within the four types of karma.
The final three repetitions explain mixed karma (*miśrakarman*).
Regarding the statement, "Furthermore, from black-and-white karma up to the general establishment of black-and-white," the Tripiṭaka Master says:
The successive arising of moments one after another is called "arising by category" (*jātivat*).
This refers to the case where a preceding moment gives rise to a wholesome mind,
and immediately in the subsequent thought-moment, an unwholesome mind arises as its concomitant (*parivāra*).
In this context, when a wholesome mental action is accompanied by an unwholesome one, they coexist as black and white;
therefore, it is called "mixed karma. Jing says:

That is to say, within the category of a single type of sentient being, there is karma that first brings affliction and later brings benefit, or karma that first brings benefit and later brings affliction;
these are collectively subsumed as the third category of mixed karma.
Bei says:
Because there are two types of volition at the time of the remote cause (dūre-hetu),
even though there is only one karma at the time of the immediate cause (kṣaṇa-samutthāna), it is described as "mixed karma" (miśra-karma).
Furthermore, regarding the establishment [of categories] based on the differentiation of objects:
it is as if there is someone who, having exhorted others to jointly create scriptures and images,
subsequently proceeds to commit acts of encroachment or damage against those scriptures and images.
Or taking the wealth of others and practicing generosity—
these are all expressions established based on differences in the object.
Furthermore, regarding that which is established by way of intrinsic nature (svabhāva):
Since the natures of good and evil are distinct, they are established as having a single result;
yet, while one may bring about benefit in a particular instance,
it simultaneously brings about harm through another matter.
From here below, he points to specific instances.
That is to say, for example, when one harbors resentment toward a person who has committed an evil deed,
one falls into the dark category due to that anger.
To take no delight in those evils and to give rise to revulsion is wholesome;
it falls within the category of the white portion (*śuklapakṣa*).
This is the thirteenth [topic]: understanding that phenomena possess causes and effects.
First, the phenomena that possess causes and possess effects are distinguished;
subsequently, by way of inversion, those that do not possess causes and do not possess effects are revealed.
Within the former, the phenomena that possess causes are first distinguished.
Regarding the subsequent discussion on dharmas that possess results,
it was stated in the preceding section:
"Furthermore, defiled abiding, the arising of wrong diligence, and fruitless toil are called 'dharmas with causes'."
It is said that non-Buddhists dwell in defilement by relying on those false teachers and false teachings;
taking this as their cause, they give rise to such states as dwelling in false diligence, fruitless toil, and sorrowful suffering.
That is to say, wrong diligence and so forth are called "dharmas with causes.
A disciple of the Buddha, relying on the Buddha’s True Dharma, is said to dwell in reliance on the undefiled.
There is right diligence, and through the exertion that bears fruit, there arises the dwelling in joy and bliss.
It is stated that right effort and so forth are called "dharmas with causes.
Furthermore, the worldly path that leads toward detachment and is capable of inducing the dhyānas and formless attainments is,
in this sense, explained as the conventional path.
Subduing the desires of the lower stages serves as the inducing cause for attaining the fruit of disjunction— the analytical cessation— of those [desires].
Furthermore, through the abandonment of desire, one attains the fundamental dhyānas and the formless attainments.
These explain the conditioned dharmas consisting of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), dhyāna, and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
Next, the dharmas that possess fruits are distinguished;
therein, the phrase "two kinds of threefold dharmas" refers to this.
As previously stated regarding causes, there are three factors for both good and evil:
first, the physical support;
second, hearing the Dharma.
Third, the contemplation of resolute conviction.
Fourteenth, the exposition of dependently originated phenomena,
which refers to the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
Fifteenth, the explanation of internal phenomena (*adhyātma-dharma*).
Regarding the statement, "If, by the predominant power of this phenomenon, external distinctions such as forms, sounds,
and so forth arise," this means that by the predominant power of the five sense faculties (*pañcendriya*), the five external objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) arise.
Regarding the statement that internal phenomena (*ādhyātmika-dharma*) are so called because they can appropriate seeds:
this is a method of exposition according to their functional correspondence (*anuvartana-yukti*).
In this context, the seeds residing within the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) and consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) are designated as "internal."
Regarding the statement that the five kinds of pure form and so forth, when in meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), are called "internal phenomena" (*ādhyātmika-dharma*):
this means that the nature of the five faculties, such as the eye, as well as mind, thought, and consciousness, is internal.

Furthermore, other phenomena established by conventional designation (*prajñapti*) are also considered internal; for instance, the five objects of the senses (*viṣaya*) that support the faculties are called "internal" because they reside within one's own body.
Sixteenth, the phenomena subsumed under name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Jing says:
"That which can be obtained through growth in various respective locations."
In order to increase one's understanding of the meaning of "form" (rūpa),
he explains the meaning of form by focusing specifically on visible matter;
that which undergoes transformation and decay through contact with hands, clods of earth, and so forth.
The meaning of "form" (rūpa) is understood through its susceptibility to change and decay.
As for the remaining four aggregates, up to the four [mental] aggregates which are designated as "name" (nāma),
this is because various names are applied to all phenomena.
The four aggregates, depending on name, tend toward all phenomena;
because they are designated by speech based on that [name],
the four aggregates are subsumed under "name."
Based on the preceding text, there are two explanations:
namely, that one seeks out all phenomena by relying on names through verbal expression,
and that one apprehends all phenomena by relying on those four aggregates.
Therefore, the four aggregates are called "name" (*nāman*) by way of analogy.
According to the two explanations, the four aggregates take up all phenomena by relying on conventional designations (*vyavahāra-nāman*);
they do so from those very conventional designations upon which they depend.
Therefore, the four aggregates are called "name" (*nāman*).
In this context, they shall be explained later.
T'ai says:
By the power of the designation through various names,
phrases, and syllables, and because these various names, phrases, and syllables serve as the basis for the four aggregates,
the mental consciousness— excepting the five sensory consciousnesses— flows toward and engages with their respective objects of perception.
Because they are able to take objects as their cognitive domain primarily through the power of names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and syllables (*vyañjana*),
the four aggregates are called "name" (*nāma*);
this designation is derived from the feeling (*vedanā*) that serves as their basis.
Although the five consciousnesses and the four aggregates do not depend on names when they take objects as their conditions,
they are all described as "name" (nāma) from the perspective of the predominant mental consciousness (manovijñāna).
Seventeenth, the exposition on the dharmas that are appropriated (*upātta*) and those that are not appropriated (*anupātta*).
Herein, the establishment of the appropriated is briefly set forth by way of five characteristics;
the first three are easily understood.
The transformation resulting from four causes and conditions, up to the objects of focus for erroneous or correct deliberation, constitutes the fourth.
Furthermore, that which is termed "transformation" refers to that which acts either to harm or to benefit.
This is the fifth characteristic.
Because it can be diminished or increased, it is called "transformation";
therefore, it is termed "appropriated" (upātta).
Thus, regarding the five characteristics mentioned below:
if form is the first,
then the internal [feeling] is the second.
If the mind and mental factors and so forth constitute the third [category],
then by such a lower summary, the fourth and fifth are established. Thus,
eighteen elements are explained as being composed of the primary elements.
First, the great elements are determined;
subsequently, the remaining [factors] not explicitly mentioned are concluded.
Within the former, there are eight successive expositions.
First, there is a general indication of the dharmas that possess form.
Second, the meaning of the great elements (mahābhūta) and derived matter (upādāyarūpa) is explained.
Regarding the statement: "If the seeds of the various great elements are able to produce their fruits, the seeds of derived matter also produce their own fruits," and so forth.
Although they arise simultaneously,
it is said that the four great elements (mahābhūta) produce derived matter (upādāyarūpa), because the seeds of the great elements must first produce their own fruits,
and only then do the seeds of derived matter produce their fruits.
Regarding the statement that the various seeds of the material sense faculties (rūpīndriya) and the great elements (mahābhūta) are said to "have a location":
although they lack a separate substantial entity, they are designated as having a location in accordance with their supporting faculties.
Third, this clarifies the distinction between the seeds and their manifestation.
The various forms produced by the manifest primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are not seeds of the primary elements;
the four manifest primary elements and the derived forms (*upādāyarūpa*) are mutually inseparable,
because those derived forms are produced from the primary elements as their substantial cause (*prakṛti-hetu*).
The various extensive treatises do not exist in isolation from one another, nor can they interpenetrate.

Fifth, regarding the analysis of karma by way of aggregates: there are distinctions; furthermore, even within a single, solid aggregate of matter, the sequence proceeds accordingly, as is appropriate for each case.
Jingyun stated:
Since the tangible objects produced by these [elements] have no distinct substance apart from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), they are not discussed separately.
As for water, fire, and so forth, they are only able to perform their functions when further conditions are awaited.
It is like when iron that has been heated by fire leaks as water;
or, as it is said, "if one encounters its momentum, it is just like water," etc.
Thus, within a mass of solid matter (*rūpa-skandha*), only this element (*dhātu*) is capable of performing the functional activity of creating derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*).
If, within a solid aggregate of matter in the desire realm,
there are also the derived matters of the three bases— form, odor, and taste—
they are likewise produced by the primary elements of that same level.
Within the solid aggregate of matter in the form realm,
there exists only the functional activity of the form realm as its support, but no odors or tastes. Within this solid aggregate,
with the exception of the elements of water, fire, wind, and the element of sound, there is only that which is pursued by seeds.
If one follows the Sautrāntika interpretation,
a solid mass of matter possesses the potential to produce water, fire, wind, and sound,
serving as the seed for these through skillful craftsmanship.
Now, following the Mahāyāna and interpreting it according to the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* in the manner of the Sautrāntika school:
according to the ultimate meaning, the solid aggregate of matter does not exist apart from the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
This fundamental consciousness possesses the seeds for the production of water, fire, wind, and so forth.
Therefore, it is also said that the solid aggregate of matter possesses seeds.
Within the nominal and conceptual aggregates of water, fire, and wind,
the sequence for the desire and form realms is likewise explained according to what is appropriate, just as in the case of the great element of earth in the solid aggregate of matter.
In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the aggregates of fire and water possess visible form, odor, and taste;
in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there is only the aggregate of wind which possesses visible form.
In the desire realm, there may also be instances where only odor exists.
In the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), wind consists exclusively of color and fragrance.
As for the statement that "within an internal aggregate of matter" and so forth, as explained at length in the Sūtra,
this does not mean that a single atom (*paramāṇu*) possesses all four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Within a single body, blood is water;
movement is wind;
and heat is fire.
"Solidity is earth.
This is the same as the scriptural passage cited in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Treatise on the Treasury) during the analysis of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Sixth, it is explained that both the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and the derived tangibles (*upādāyarūpa*) are all substantial entities (*rūpa-dravya*).
Seventh, explaining the underlying intent (*abhiprāya*) of the Sūtra:
The Blessed One further stated that "contact" refers to the external bases (*bāhyāyatana*), whether they be the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) or derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*).
What is the underlying intent here?

Answer: Regarding these primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and the various distinctions such as roughness and smoothness that have been explained—just as it was said that roughness and so forth arise because of the predominance of earth and wind—these are merely designated by the names "rough" and so on as provisional constructs (*prajñapti*) based on the functional power of the four great elements; they do not constitute [separate] categories of their own kind.
"Arising as a different category" refers to the five faculties, such as the eye, excluding the faculty of touch;
and the four objects, excluding touch, which exist apart from these four great elements (mahābhūta), namely the nine bases (*āyatana*) and a portion of the base of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
Heterogeneous elements act as creators in contrast to heterogeneous derived matter;
thus, it is said that homogeneous elements act as creators of their own kind of derived matter.
Furthermore, whether it be the Buddha or Buddhadeva, they maintain that all derived matter is composed of the great elements and possesses the characteristic of tangibility.
Now, since this sutra states that "tangibility" refers to the great elements (mahābhūta) and their derivatives (upādāya-rūpa) among the external bases,
and does not state that there are nine other real forms (rūpa) existing separately from tangibility,
how can the Master [Vasubandhu], in his Mahayana school, claim that among the eleven types of form, only tangibility is composed of the four great elements?
Are the other nine material elements not likewise composed of atoms?
This is now explained for clarification:
this sutra merely speaks of their own respective categories within the common locus of the tangible.
If the sphere of tangibility is a derivative [form],
it is conventionally established based upon those primary elements;
as for the other nine derivative forms, they are not conventionally established based upon the primary elements.
"Why does the Buddha state that 'contact' refers to the external sense base (bāhyāyatana) as being derived from the four great elements (mahābhūta),
yet does not say that there is some other form (rūpa) distinct from the external [elements]?
This is the question posed by Buddhadeva.
He establishes that outside the four great elements there is nothing that is not distinct;
all derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) is subsumed within the sphere of the tangible (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*),
for it possesses eight characteristics as its determinate object.

Question: Since the preceding treatise has already explained that the matter of mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi-vaśitā-rūpa*) exists, by which four great elements (*mahābhūta*) is it produced?
Answer: It is produced by the four great elements of whichever level of meditative concentration the mind arises from.
In this treatise, it is stated that the reflected image-form (*pratibimba-rūpa*) is composed of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) which serve as its objective basis (*ālambana*).
However, the preceding treatise further states that this reflected image-form arises from the meditative mind (*samādhi-citta*) and is not composed of the primary elements.
Regarding the contradiction among these three points, if one asks how they are to be reconciled,
the explanation is as follows: what was previously stated— that it is not composed of the four great elements— is [the intended meaning].
This is a statement that exhausts the reasoning.
Because the form produced by meditative concentration arises from the mind and is not a phenomenon characterized by resistance,
it is not derived from the primary elements.
Now, when it is said that from the substantial matter of the object of cognition (*ālambana*) there arises a single reflected image (*pratibimba-rūpa*) produced by the primary elements (*mahābhūta*),
this is stated with reference to a remote condition;
for the reflected image arises through the contemplation of that substantial basis.
Therefore, this statement was made.
As for the previous passage stating that [the body] is derived from the great elements of the same level as the meditative mind that observes it,
this was said in reference to its immediate conditions.
This means that by means of a concentrated mind, the four great elements of that same level arise;
because they exist simultaneously and in the same location as the reflected form, it is said figuratively that [the mind] "creates" them.
In reality, however, it does not create them.
Although there are these three explanations, they do not contradict one another.
Regarding the nineteenth interpretation of the "existent dharma," the middle passage states:
"As the World-Honored One asked, up to the point where he spoke these words."
The Buddha taught that for ordinary persons and those in training, the contaminated worldly dharmas of the three realms— which have not yet been abandoned and ought to be abandoned—
are called "contaminated" (*sāsrava*).
This concludes the twentieth [section], the explanation of dharmas with a superior and dharmas without a superior.
These five meanings explain that it is nirvāṇa and the unsurpassed dharma.
Through these five causes,
other dharmas— whether in greater or lesser measure— are entirely devoid of them and are therefore not called "unsurpassed."
Among the five causes, the first two possess the remaining [factors] respectively;
the next two pertain to both [types]; and the last one is without remainder.
There are twenty-one dharmas that should be cultivated.
Regarding the "four cultivations," they are mostly explained from the perspective of a single entity.
The Tripiṭaka Master says:
"Setting aside the contemplation of twenty people as a collective, the aspect of impurity manifests before one."
The non-appearance of the pure aspects of the essential image is called the cultivation of removal (*apanayana-bhāvanā*).
Furthermore, through the power of contemplation and the power of removal,
one eliminates the heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) of body and mind and attains their pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
This is called the cultivation of removal (*vibhāvanā-bhāvanā*).

As for the statement in the text that it is called the cultivation of removal because one eliminates and severs unwholesome mental attention (*akuśala-manasikāra*) that has already arisen: [this refers to the process of abandoning what has already occurred].
In this fourth cultivation of the antidotes, there are four types of antidotes.
These are to be correlated with the seven mental engagements (*manasikāra*) that follow.

It should be understood that among these, from the "mental engagement of discerning characteristics" up to the "mental engagement of conviction," they are called the cultivation of the antidote of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇā-pratipakṣa*).
The third is the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) that observes the characteristics of phenomena.
From "separation" up to "the culmination of skillful means," these are termed the cultivation of the antidote of abandonment (*prahāṇapratipakṣabhāvanā*);
therein, there are three types of mental attention (*manasikāra*).
This refers to the culmination of the skillful means for withdrawing from attachment to pleasure.
The mental attention regarding the fruit is called the cultivation of maintaining the antidote.
From this point upward, all seven types of mental attention are subsumed under the superior stages and higher stages.
The previous explanation of the seven types of mental application (*manasikāra*) pertained to the stage of skillful means (*upāyabhūmi*);
the present explanation of the seven types of mental application concerns their progressive cultivation within the fundamental stages (*mūlabhūmi*).
It should be understood that all these are termed "cultivation as a remedy for distancing" (*dūrībhāvapratipakṣabhāvanā*).
The seven types of mental attention, when compared to what was previously abandoned, serve as a distant prevention;
they are all "distant-part" (dūrabhāga) antidotes that, in relation to what was previously abandoned,
act as a distant prevention.
From this point downward, the four types of cultivation are collectively categorized into two:
namely, the cultivation of guarding and upholding, and the cultivation of mental attention.
From this point downward, these two are further expanded into four.
In this context, what is called the cultivation of the body refers to the cultivation of protection;
contemplating the impurity of the body is termed the cultivation of the body,
which is identical to the third aforementioned cultivation of removal.
Regarding the cultivation of ethical discipline (*śīla*), "cultivation" refers to its reception and maintenance.
Guarding the six sense faculties is called the cultivation of the foundation;
this is the aforementioned fourth cultivation of counteractive measures (*pratipakṣa-bhāvanā*).
If the cultivation of attention belonging to the dhyāna stages is called "cultivation of the mind," this refers to the first type mentioned above,
the cultivation of acquisition (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*).
If the cultivation of knowledge through the clear realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*) is called "cultivation of wisdom" (*prajñā-bhāvanā*), [this refers to the second type].
This is the second stage of cultivation mentioned previously:
the twenty-two ways of understanding the dharmas of the three periods of time.
Regarding the understanding of the past, this first section provides a general analysis of the dharmas of the past.
The matter will be explained separately later.
In the preceding section, there are six phrases. The first is:
"the causes have already been exhausted."
1. The substance of the two fruits has already ceased. 2.
Subsequent dharmas produced by conditions arise, excluding the final aggregate. 3.

The causal function is not lost, ensuring that the fruit will eventually ripen. 4. [The causal function is not lost, ensuring that the fruit will eventually ripen. (Note: The fourth point is a repetition of the third in the source text).
Fifth, mindfulness arises with respect to the object.
Sixth, it is manifested solely by cessation and has no separate entity;
the future is understood as "attainment."
This refers to seeds.
The remainder of the text may be understood accordingly.
Twenty-three [categories] explain the phenomena bound to the three realms.
Regarding the first point concerning the explanation that the mind of the desire realm does not abide in meditative concentration:

this means that even at the time of entering meditative absorption, there are still sense faculties, objects, and the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), which are not factors belonging to the stage of concentration;
however, because these are not present in their entirety, they are omitted from the description.
Alternatively, it may be that the concentrated mind itself is called "in concentration," while other dharmas in this state are not so designated.
This explains the phrase "or arising from concentration" found within the description of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
This refers to the twenty-four types of knowledge, such as the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇa-citta*) and so forth, which understand phenomena according to their three natures (*tri-svabhāva*).
Among these, the names and meanings are first distinguished, followed by the establishment of their specific classifications.
If, among the aforementioned [states], there is contaminated wholesome [karma] that subdues various inversions and leads to rebirth as a human or a deva,
or if there is uncontaminated wholesome [karma] that eradicates all inversions and realizes nirvana,
both are therefore termed "secure."
Within the section on "Establishing the Distinctions," that which is called "pure dwelling" should refer to the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*).
Furthermore, regarding the statement that among all wholesome dharmas, those accomplished through giving up to those consisting of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) are superior:
three are mutually compared, while the latter two are consistently inferior because they are situated below.
Because it exists within [the path],
it is superior to giving but inferior to cultivation;
since cultivation is the most supreme, it is invariably superior to the former two.
Regarding the statement, "In this context, 'neutral by nature' refers to the various material sense organs (*indriya*) and so forth," Jing says:
"This includes the five sense organs that are nurtured (*aupacayika*), as well as the five non-sentient sense objects (*viṣaya*)."
The five sense objects that support the faculties are all subsumed under the category of intrinsic indeterminate (*svabhāva-avyākṛta*).
The phrase "not subsumed under maturation (*vipāka*) and so forth" includes,
by the term "and so forth," the five sense objects of deportment (*airyāpathika*), craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), and transformation (*nairmāṇika*).
It is not excluded because it is indeterminate by nature (*svabhāva-avyākṛta*).
Tai says:
"Among those that are indeterminate by nature, only its matter (*rūpa*) is indicated."
Therefore, it is known that mind is comprised solely of the four types of indeterminate (*avyākṛta*);
there is no fifth indeterminate. Ji says:
The attachment to dharmas within the sixth and seventh consciousnesses is also termed "innate indeterminate" (*svabhāva-avyākṛta*);
therefore, it pervades the five aggregates.
[Section] Twenty-five: Explaining the Dharmas of the Three Trainings.
The wholesome states of the seven preparatory stages (prayoga) prior to the path of seeing through the principle of insight are also subsumed under "training" (śaikṣa).
Now, this general judgment concerns the phenomena of the three natures (trisvabhāva) accomplished by ordinary beings (pṛthagjana);
all of these are categorized as "neither."
Regarding the twenty-sixth [section], the explanation of the three types of abandonment (*prahāṇadharma*):
the phrase "karma leading to rebirth in evil destinies and so forth" refers specifically to the bodily karma of a woman.
The karma for the eighth existence, the karma of Uttarakuru,
and the karma of the Unconscious Heaven (asaṃjñisattva-deva)—
all these are included among those abandoned by insight (darśana-heya) that are described as "entirely non-obscured" (anivṛta).

Question: Since the preceding treatise has already stated that at the time of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), all aggregates, elements, and bases (*skandha-dhātu-āyatana*) pertaining to the evil destinies are abandoned, why is it stated here again that those which are non-obscured and neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) are all abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*)?
The commentary states:
The preceding [passage] was based on the extinction of causes and the consequent loss of thought;
therefore, it was said that all aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and bases (āyatana) of the evil destinies are abandoned through the path of seeing (darśanamārga).
Now, based on the nature of the aggregates, there exists the bondage of conditions;
since this bondage must be severed by means of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), there is no contradiction.
This is the twenty-seventh [topic]: the explanation of the profound and difficult-to-perceive dharmas.
The meaning is that all phenomena are profound because their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are inexpressible;
for example, the specific characteristic of form is realized only by visual consciousness,
and so on, up to the characteristic of tangibility, which is realized only by tactile consciousness.
It is like drinking cold water;
only the one who has realized it knows that it cannot be described in words.
To describe its characteristics is in every way inadequate to the reality.
As a skillful means for guidance,
when teaching the various dharmas, one speaks only of their common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*);
for example, when speaking of form (*rūpa*), it is referred to by such names as "form."
Because it characterizes all forms, it is a common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*);
the same applies to sound and so forth.
Therefore, a phenomenon as a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) cannot be expressed in words.
